title: What's the deal with phantom pain?
summary: Josh and Chuck explain phantom limb pain: pain felt in a limb that has been amputated, how it differs from residual limb pain and phantom limb sensation, and its history from Ambrose Paré (mid-1500s) through Descartes, William Porterfield (1759), Silas Weir Mitchell's Civil War-era work and the fictional "Case of George Deadlow," and later psychological misattributions. They cover current theories (neuroma, neuroplasticity, appropriated reception/body map theory), the mirror box, and treatments including prosthetics with sensory feedback, targeted muscle reinnervation, TENS, biofeedback and drugs. The episode opens with holiday travel banter and closes with listener mail about teaching children about race and science.
topics: Stuff You Should Know listener mail

segments.title: Opening banter and travel talk
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck chat about recent family trips to Disney World, Universal Studios and Hawaii, and a Smashmouth-style video cameo by Ken Marino, before turning to the episode topic.

segments.title: What phantom limb pain is
segments.summary: The hosts define phantom limb pain as pain felt in an amputated limb, distinct from residual limb pain in the stump and from phantom limb sensation. They describe the range of pain types people report and note its psychological and quality-of-life impact.

segments.title: Ambrose Paré and early history
segments.summary: Ambrose Paré, a sixteenth-century French surgeon, is credited with first describing phantom limb pain and distinguishing it from residual limb pain. He proposed causes in nerves of the residual limb or in the brain. Descartes and William Porterfield, who described his own amputation in 1759, followed.

segments.title: Civil War amputations and Silas Weir Mitchell
segments.summary: Amputations during the American Civil War brought renewed attention to the condition. Silas Weir Mitchell first wrote a fictional story, The Case of George Dedlow, which was taken seriously by some readers, then published a real scientific account reporting high rates of phantom pain among patients.

segments.title: Psychological misattribution and mistreatment
segments.summary: Through the mid-twentieth century many doctors attributed phantom pain to psychological causes and personality traits. The hosts say a 1997 or later meta-analysis finally established that patients were not psychologically disturbed, and describe harsh historical treatments.

segments.title: First-person accounts and syndrome question
segments.summary: Olivia's research uncovered Norwegian case reports describing phantom limbs stuck in odd positions, a toe nail growing into another toe, and burning skin sensations. The hosts discuss how persistent pain is a constant reminder of the amputation.

segments.title: Causes: neuromas, body map and neuroplasticity
segments.summary: The hosts review leading theories: neuroma formation at severed nerve ends, the appropriated reception (body map) theory, and neuroplasticity with cortical rewiring. They also cover recent findings challenging the neuroplasticity explanation and the mirror box research by V.S. Ramachandran, whose benefits appear short-term.

segments.title: Prosthetics, nerve reinnervation and treatments
segments.summary: Research on advanced prosthetics that send sensory feedback, targeted muscle reinnervation, and sensory reinnervation is discussed as promising. Other treatments mentioned include TENS, biofeedback, distraction, massage, lifestyle changes and pain medication.

segments.title: Listener mail on teaching children about race
segments.summary: A listener, a researcher on race and racism who is Professor Laughter at the University of Tennessee, writes that children should learn both the science of human variation and that racism is a social construct. The hosts thank them.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Josh closes the episode and gives the podcast's contact information.
